analysis.one_liner: Repeals the charge on methane emissions from large oil and gas facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill to repeal the methane emissions charge and the EPA's methane reduction program has sat without action in the House Energy and Commerce Committee since January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would erase Section 136 of the Clean Air Act, which does two things: it runs a program where the EPA supports efforts to cut methane leaks from oil and gas operations, and it charges a fee on petroleum and natural gas facilities that emit 25,000 metric tons or more of greenhouse gases a year. It would also cancel any money not yet spent under that program. Introduced by Rep. August Pfluger with five Republican cosponsors, it was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and has stayed there ever since.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, especially large producers whose facilities cross the 25,000-ton annual emissions threshold and would owe the methane charge. Repeal would remove the per-ton cost of excess methane emissions and eliminate a program that funds leak-detection and repair efforts in their sector.

how_it_helps.text: It eliminates the charge on methane emissions from petroleum and natural gas systems facilities that emit 25,000 metric tons or more of greenhouse gases per year, removing a direct cost on those companies' excess emissions.
It repeals the EPA's methane emissions and waste reduction incentive program for the oil and gas sector, ending federal support for reducing methane from those operations.
It rescinds any unobligated funds already made available under the program, so the money would no longer be available for methane-reduction projects.

analysis.who_pays: The public bears the cost: methane is a potent greenhouse gas, so removing the fee and the support program means more leaks go unfixed, warming accelerates, and federal revenue from the charge is lost. Communities near oil and gas facilities face the most direct exposure to those emissions.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone exposed to methane pollution and lost revenue

drawbacks.text: Repealing the charge removes the financial penalty for oil and gas facilities that waste or vent methane, weakening the incentive to detect and repair leaks.
It ends a federal program that provides support for reducing methane emissions from the oil and gas sector, taking away help for cleanup projects.
It rescinds unobligated program funds, so money set aside for methane reduction would be pulled back rather than spent.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit goes narrowly to oil and gas producers, who would stop paying for excess methane emissions, while the costs — more unchecked methane, a canceled federal cleanup program, and lost federal revenue — are spread across everyone else. Because methane is a powerful driver of warming, the trade weighs clearly in favor of the industry and against the public.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee in January 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. August Pfluger introduced the Natural Gas Tax Repeal Act in the House on January 9, 2025.
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day, and the committee has held no markup or vote on it since.
Five Republican representatives cosponsored the bill; no Democrats did.
If enacted, the bill would repeal Section 136 of the Clean Air Act, eliminating both the EPA's methane emissions reduction support program and the charge on large oil and gas facilities.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill never advanced, the methane charge on large oil and gas facilities and the EPA's methane reduction program remain in place, so people exposed to methane pollution are better off than they would have been if it had passed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Communities near gas facilities; the fee stays

for.name: Rep. August Pfluger
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Clean Air Act methane program and emissions charge.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action; no markup, hearing vote, or floor consideration has occurred.

sides.party_line_note: All six sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans; no Democrat supported the bill and no vote has been held to test it further.

industries.note: The bill would eliminate a per-ton charge on methane emissions from large petroleum and natural gas facilities and end the EPA program supporting methane cleanup in the sector. The companies avoid a pollution cost while the public absorbs the warming and local air-quality consequences.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action more than a year after referral and only six Republican supporters, the bill is likely to remain in the Energy and Commerce Committee unless party leadership chooses to prioritize a methane repeal, which a simple introduction and referral do not signal.
